cim: Trump floats 'tremendous tax' on companies that build data centers overseas
cim_eredeti: Trump floats 'tremendous tax' on companies that build data centers overseas
szoveg_eredeti:

President Donald Trump is threatening to impose steep taxes on companies that build data centers abroad, as those projects face backlash from many communities in the United States.

President Trump framed the proposal as part of a broader competition with China on artificial intelligence, which the president refers to as "super intelligence." It comes on the heels of an overseas trip that showcased his relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

During a White House press briefing recapping his travels on Friday, Trump told reporters, "We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen, and we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it."

The details of the policy weren't immediately clear. Trump described the proposal as a "breaking story" during the briefing.

"I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said.

Trump also urged Americans to use data center construction as an opportunity to extract concessions from developers.

"You're going to make a lot of money. You're going to have your taxes reduced. They're going to build their own electricity, so the electricity is going to go down," Trump said.

Trump has generally resisted calls to regulate AI, arguing that such guardrails could hurt America's competitive edge against China, but he's backing a bipartisan bill that, in part, aims to require data centers to cover their own energy costs and grid upgrades, rather than passing those costs on to consumers through higher utility bills. That bill is heading to the House after it won approval in the Senate on Thursday, despite concerns from some environmental advocates.

Meanwhile, Trump said he discussed some AI safeguards with Chinese President Xi Jinping during his trip. Trump didn't offer specifics during Friday's briefing, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that both sides agreed that major military operations using AI should not happen without human involvement.

Bessent was also asked about the Trump administration's recent move to block China's remote access to America's most advanced semiconductor chips, which are at the center of the global AI race. He said that no further restrictions are needed on the sale of older chips made by Nvidia, even as some critics argue that the administration should be doing more to protect sensitive American technology.

The ability of Chinese tech firms to access American-made chips came under renewed scrutiny after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following extramarital affair allegations, including with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

"He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person," Trump said Friday. " I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance."
